title: Alma Tharp Joins Memminger High School Victory Corps — World War II Community Service
description:
Newspaper article announcing the formation of a Victory Corps unit at Memminger High School in Charleston, South Carolina, as part of the school's contribution to the World War II home-front effort. The program was designed to train high-school students for future war service while encouraging active participation in community wartime activities.

Students were required to meet academic, physical-training and community-service standards. Activities included Red Cross work, Civilian Defense assistance, USO support, rationing-board work, selling war bonds and stamps, victory gardens, and other wartime service projects.

Among the students listed as enrolling in the Victory Corps is Alma Thorp [Tharp], who attended Memminger High School before becoming known for her aviation activities and membership in The Ninety-Nines.

title: Alma Tharp Serves in Memminger Victory Corps Nurses Aides Squad
description:
Newspaper article reporting the organization and officers of the Memminger Victory Corps at Memminger High School in Charleston, South Carolina. The corps was divided into specialized squads supporting community and wartime service activities, including the USO, Victory Gardens, Red Cross, clerical and library work, and nurses' aide service.

Alma Tharp is specifically listed as a member of the First Platoon Nurses Aides Squad, along with Marie Petit, Sylvia Ginsberg, Virginia Burdashaw, Eloise Adams, Edna Hill, and Helen Hill.

The article notes that Victory Corps members drilled each Tuesday under the direction of M. Simon Fogarty and Mr. Utsey of the Home Guard. Girls who completed 25 hours of community service and physical fitness work were presented with official Victory Corps insignia.

title: Alma Tharp Receives Private Pilot License
description: Newspaper clipping reporting that Alma Tharp of Folly Beach, South Carolina, qualified for her private pilot license at Carolina Skyways Airport. William S. Scott was president of Carolina Skyways.

title: Alma Tharp Among “Queens” Welcoming Pilots — April 12–14, 1945
description:
Newspaper photograph showing a group of young women gathered around visiting pilots during an aviation event in April 1945. The surviving portion of the caption begins “QUEENS SURROUND PILOTS” and identifies pilots Clifford Evans Jr. and George Truman; the remainder of the original caption is not visible in this scan.

This clipping was preserved among Alma Tharp's aviation and personal memorabilia and appears to relate to her early involvement in aviation activities while still a teenager. The filename associated with the clipping dates the event or newspaper material to April 12–14, 1945.

Alma Tharp Memorabilia — Clemson Dances and Middleton Place Gardens
description:
Collection of personal keepsakes preserved among Alma Edythe Tharp's papers, including two invitations from The Central Dance Association at Clemson, South Carolina, and an admission pass to Middleton Place Gardens near Charleston.

The Clemson invitations are for an Autumn Ball, held November 21–22 at the College Fieldhouse with music by Billy Knauff, and a Rat Hop, held October 3–4 at the College Fieldhouse with music by The Jungaleers. The invitations specify formal or semi-formal Friday-night dances followed by informal Saturday-night events.

The Middleton Place Gardens pass is handwritten for “Miss Alma Tharp and one guest” and appears to have been issued on a complimentary basis.

title: Alma Tharp at Folly Beach — Miss American Legion Beauty Contest and Mr. Folly Beach
description:
Two newspaper clippings documenting Alma Tharp's involvement in Folly Beach community events. In the first, “22 Young Women Will Seek Legion Beauty Title at Folly Pier,” Alma Tharp of Folly Beach is named Master of Ceremonies for the Miss American Legion Beauty contest at Folly Pier, sponsored by Palmetto Post 112.

The second article, “Women Scream and Cheer As Muscle Men Flex Biceps,” reports on a Mr. Folly Beach physique contest held at Folly Pier. Rembert Garris, a 22-year-old Charleston YMCA bodybuilder, won the competition and was presented with the trophy by Miss Folly Beach, Alma Thorp [Tharp], whom he kissed during the presentation.

title: Alma Edythe Tharp and William Burnett McDowell Jr.
description:
Engagement announcement for Alma Edythe Tharp, and William Burnett McDowell Jr., of Shelton, South Carolina. The article notes that both Alma and William were devoted to flying, held private pilot licenses, and were working toward commercial and instructor licenses. 

She did not show up to the wedding. Her family and everyone else were there. She ran off to Annie Bell's home and hid out there.

title: Alma Tharp Flies to Carolina Ninety-Nines Annual Convention
description: Alma Tharp flies to Carolinas Ninety-Nines convention, Spartanburg, S.C, for a two-day annual convention of the Carolinas Chapter of the Ninety-Nines. Alma Tharp flew from Charleston to Spartanburg in her nearly new Ercoupe.

title: Carolina Ninety-Nines Annual Meeting in Spartanburg
description: Spartanburg, South Carolina. Newspaper announcement of the annual meeting of the Carolinas Chapter of the Ninety-Nines, the international organization of women pilots. Members were scheduled to gather in Spartanburg for a weekend meeting, including a buffet supper and the chapter's annual business meeting at the Cleveland Hotel. The article lists “Alma Thorpe” of Charleston, apparently a newspaper misspelling of Alma Tharp, along with fellow Charleston pilot Jewell Bailey.

description: Circa 1948. Alma Tharp, at left, with another woman beside an Ercoupe aircraft. Alma was an active member of the Carolinas Chapter of the Ninety-Nines and a licensed private pilot. A contemporary newspaper account records Alma flying her nearly new Ercoupe from Charleston to Spartanburg for a Carolinas Ninety-Nines convention. title: Charleston Azalea Festival Parade — Folly Beach delegation / Alma Tharp — 1948
Folly Beach Float Wins at Tenth Annual Azalea Festival — Alma Tharp Represented as Queen
description:
Newspaper coverage of the Tenth Annual Azalea Festival parade in Charleston, South Carolina, attended by an estimated 80,000 spectators. More than 100 beauty representatives, including 28 official queens, participated along with 25 floats, 11 bands, and other parade units.

The Folly Beach float, on which Alma Tharp served as queen, was judged the winning entry in the towns category. The article describes the float as featuring a large silver-and-green fan and identifies Alma's attendants as June Lockwood, Rose Marie Frost, Mary Lou Barnett, and Stella Barnett. Delores Jowers and Ann Angel rode at the front of the float.

The accompanying article, “Queens Have Really Busy Day Ahead,” describes the schedule of activities arranged for the festival's 28 official queens, including a press conference, visits to Charleston's gardens, a hospital appearance, luncheon, and participation in festival events.

title: lma Tharp Rides on Prize-Winning Folly Beach Float — Azalea Festival, 1948
description:
Newspaper photograph of the Folly Beach entry in the 1948 Azalea Festival parade. The elaborate float, designed by Clinton Thompson and Mrs. Marion Murphy, was judged best in the towns classification.

The float featured a large silver-and-green fan and carried several young women representing Folly Beach. The newspaper caption specifically identifies Alma Tharp, along with June Lockwood, Rose Marie Frost, Mary Lou Barnett, and Stella Barnett, as the “Folly Beach beauties” riding on the float. Delores Jowers, Ann Angel, and Harry Bishop rode painted merry-go-round horses at the front.

title: Alma Tharp Named Queen of Folly Beach Azalea Festival Float
description:
Collection of newspaper clippings and photographs documenting Alma Tharp's selection as Queen of the Folly Beach Azalea Festival float. Alma, identified as the 21-year-old daughter of G. E. Tharp of Folly Beach, won a beauty contest and dance held at the Folly Beach Community Center and was chosen to ride in the place of honor on the community's Azalea Festival parade float.

Her court consisted of June Lockwood, runner-up; Rose Marie Frost; Mary Lou Barnett; and Stella Barnett. One article identifies Burnette Spencer as Alma's secretary during the event and reports that Alma was crowned by contest judge C. Wayne Cox.

The clippings also provide important biographical details about Alma. She was a graduate of Memminger High School, was employed by the Hay Oil Company, owned her own airplane, and held a private pilot's license.

The accompanying photographs show Alma wearing her crown and formal gown following her selection as Miss Folly Beach and Queen of the Folly Beach Azalea Festival float.

title: Alma Tharp Wins Folly Beach Beauty and Popularity Contest
description:
Two related newspaper clippings document a James Island Parent-Teacher Association game party and popularity contest held at the Folly Beach Community Center for girls and babies from James Island and Folly Beach.

The follow-up article, “Miss Alma Tharp Wins Beach Beauty Contest,” reports that Alma Tharp, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. G. E. Tharp of 310 East Cooper Street, Folly Beach, was named winner of the girls' popularity contest. Alma was presented with a gold pin watch as her prize.

A baby contest held at the same event was won by two-year-old Buddy Cochran, son of Mrs. Thelma Cochran of 305 Erie Avenue. He received a $5 war stamp, which he presented back to the James Island P.T.A.

title: Alma Tharp and Jewell Bailey: Charleston Women Pilots — 1948
description: November 12, 1948 newspaper feature about Charleston aviators Alma Tharp and Jewell Bailey, members of the Ninety-Nines women pilots’ organization. Alma is pictured preparing to take Jewell for a flight from Carolina Airways Airport in her airplane, “Rebel.” Published in The Charleston Evening Post.

title: Alma Tharp and The Ninety-Nines — Carolina Women Pilots and Air Race, 1949
description:
Collection of May 1949 newspaper clippings documenting Alma Tharp's aviation activities and involvement with the Carolinas Chapter of The Ninety-Nines, the international organization of licensed women pilots.
A May 21, 1949 News and Courier article records Alma receiving her private pilot license at Carolina Skyways Airport. That same weekend, Alma flew her trim Ercoupe from Charleston to Spartanburg for the Carolinas Chapter's annual meeting. Other clippings identify her alongside fellow women pilots including Jewell Bailey.
The chapter meetings included planning for the upcoming All-Woman Transcontinental Air Race, scheduled to begin in San Diego on June 11 and finish in Greenville, South Carolina. Charleston was selected as the race's eastern continental marker, requiring competitors to fly through Charleston before proceeding to Greenville.

Dates represented: May 21 and May 25, 1949.

title: John J. Tharp Jr. Earns Pilot’s License at 17
description: March 1, 1950 newspaper article featuring 17-year-old John J. Tharp Jr. of Folly Beach after earning his pilot’s license. The photograph shows his sister, aviatrix Alma Tharp, giving him some last-minute advice before he takes off in the family airplane. The article describes John as the youngest member of the Breakfast Club and notes the family’s strong connection to aviation.

title: Alma Tharp Represents Folly Beach in the Azalea Festival Parade
description: Newspaper coverage of Charleston’s Azalea Festival parade notes Alma Tharp as “Miss Folly Beach,” riding aboard the Folly Beach float with other local representatives. The article is another glimpse into Alma’s life beyond aviation, showing her involvement in Charleston-area social and community events during the early 1950s.

title: Alma Tharp Attends Ninety-Nines Meeting for 1950 Women’s Transcontinental Air Race
description: 1950 — Charleston, South Carolina. Alma Tharp of Folly Beach attended a quarterly meeting of the Carolinas Chapter of the Ninety-Nines at Charleston Municipal Airport. Members discussed plans for the annual All-Woman Transcontinental Air Race, scheduled to begin in San Diego on June 11 and finish in Greenville, South Carolina, with Charleston serving as the eastern continental marker. The article lists Alma among the Carolinas Ninety-Nines members attending the meeting.

title: Ninety-Nines Women Pilots, 1950
description:
Newspaper clippings and a Carolinas Chapter newsletter document Alma Tharp of Folly Beach, South Carolina, as an active member of The Ninety-Nines, the international organization of licensed women pilots. In 1950, Alma was described as the youngest member of the Southeastern section of the two Carolinas. She and fellow Charleston pilot Jewell Bailey represented the organization at aviation events and conventions, including the Southeastern convention in Brunswick, Georgia, and had previously served as hostesses at the national Ninety-Nines convention in Greenville.

The Carolinas Chapter newsletter also identifies Alma as a “99er from Charleston” and reports that she won a prize at an S.C. Breakfast Club meeting at Newberry for flying the greatest distance to attend. Together, the items document Alma's active participation in South Carolina aviation and the organized community of women pilots during 1950.

Dates visible on the archive page: May 31, 1950 and September 5, 1950.

The article notes that Alma was selected as one of the hostesses for the organization’s national convention and was employed by Kerrison’s department store as an assistant buyer in lingerie.

title: Aviatrix Wed — Alma Edythe Tharp Marries James Stewart “Buster” Bell Jr.
description:
Newspaper announcement of the marriage of Alma Edythe Tharp of Folly Beach, South Carolina, to James Stewart Bell Jr. of Lancaster, South Carolina, on April 28 at Heath Springs. Alma, a graduate of Memminger High School, had been flying for six years, owned her own airplane, and held a private pilot’s license. She was a member of the Charleston Civil Air Patrol and was described as the youngest member in the Carolinas of The Ninety-Nines, an international organization of women pilots.

James Stewart Bell Jr., son of Mrs. James S. Bell and the late Mr. Bell of Lancaster, had served four years in the U.S. Marines and was employed at Grace Bleachery in Lancaster, where the couple planned to live.

title: Carolina Women Pilots Hold Gathering at Folly Beach — Alma Tharp Hosts Ninety-Nines
description:
Newspaper article and group photograph documenting a quarterly meeting of the Carolinas Chapter of the Southeastern Section of The Ninety-Nines, the international organization of licensed women pilots. The gathering was held at Folly Beach, South Carolina, with Alma Tharp of Charleston serving as hostess at her home.

The article identifies Alma as a 19-year-old private pilot who had been flying for approximately two and a half years, was working toward her commercial pilot license, and hoped to own a new Cub Cruiser. Members traveled to the meeting from across South and North Carolina, with several arriving by airplane at Carolina Skyways Airport on James Island.

The accompanying photograph identifies Alma among the women pilots. Kneeling, left to right: Mrs. Burnette Spencer of High Point, N.C.; Alma Tharp, hostess; and Jewell Bailey of Charleston.

title: Lancaster Girl Pilot Proves Woman’s Place Is in Airplane — Alma Bell and Her Ercoupe
description:
The Lancaster News profile of Alma Edythe Tharp Bell (Mrs. Buster Bell) of Lancaster, South Carolina, describing her extensive involvement in aviation. The article reports that Alma had been flying since age 14, had accumulated approximately 500 flying hours, and at age 24 was teaching her husband, James Stewart “Buster” Bell Jr., to fly in preparation for his pilot’s license.

Alma owned an Ercoupe two-seat airplane and was the only Lancaster woman known to belong to The Ninety-Nines, the international organization of licensed women pilots. She had been a member for five years and also belonged to the Civil Air Patrol and the South Carolina Breakfast Club. The article recalls that Alma's father initially objected to her interest in flying but later took lessons himself, obtained his pilot's license, and bought an airplane.

At the time of the article, Alma and Buster were living at 407 East Gay Street in Lancaster. Alma worked in the order department of Springs Cotton Mills and continued flying with Buster on weekends.

title: William “Dickey” Bell — First Grade Report Card, Erwin School, 1962–1963
description:
First-grade report card for William “Dickey” Bell from Erwin School, Lancaster City Schools, Lancaster, South Carolina, for the 1962–1963 school year. His teacher was Nancy L. Graham, and the principal was Mrs. T. K. Cunningham. At the end of the year, Dickey was assigned to second grade.

Dickey earned A grades in Arithmetic, Reading, Writing, Science, and Health, with a final citizenship grade of B. The report records 180 days present, no absences, and no tardies for the school year.

His habits and attitudes were marked satisfactory in nearly every category, including completing his work, following directions, respecting others, working independently, and caring for books and property. The one recurring area marked “Needs Improvement” was controlling talking and whispering.

The report card contains several parent signatures of James S. Bell, providing an additional family record connected with Dickey's elementary-school years.

title: Farm League Tigers Defeat Dickey Bell’s Yankees, 18–12
description:
Newspaper article reporting a Farm League baseball game at Hunter Field in which the Tigers defeated the Yankees, 18–12. The Tigers, managed by Don Scott and Dick Richards, earned their second consecutive victory after losing their first eleven games. Joe Simpson was the winning pitcher, while Sam Thomas, Randy Watts, and Gary Powell led the Tigers at the plate. Ray Bowers and Larry Blackwell were the leading Yankee hitters.

The Yankees were coached by Bob Ackerman. Following the loss, the coaches and team were invited to Dickey Bell’s home, where they were treated to hot dogs to “soothe aching souls and wounded pride.”

title: Farm League Yankees Close Out Season — Dickey Bell Hosts Team Party
description:
Newspaper article describing the final weeks of the Farm League Yankees' baseball season. The Yankees defeated the Red Sox 2–1 on Tuesday and defeated the Tigers twice, 4–0 on Wednesday and 6–2 on Thursday.

On Wednesday night, Dickey Bell hosted a hot dog party at his home for the Yankees. Following Thursday's game, the team celebrated Ronnie Rogers' surprise birthday with Pepsi, cake, and ice cream.

The article also records several team outings organized by Coach Bob Ackerman. On June 26, he took the players to Charlotte, North Carolina, to watch live championship wrestling at WBTV. The Yankees then planned a trip to Atlanta on July 6 and 7 to see the Atlanta Braves play.

title: Marine Major John J. Tharp Returns Home After Being Wounded in Vietnam — March 8, 1968
description:
Globe newspaper article dated Friday, March 8, 1968, documenting the return of Marine Major John J. Tharp after he was wounded while serving as a helicopter pilot in Vietnam. Major Tharp had deployed to Vietnam in March 1967 and served with Marine Medium Helicopter Squadron HMM-165 aboard the USS Valley Forge.

During a mission supporting Marines at the Huế Citadel, Tharp was piloting a CH-46 helicopter when enemy fire struck the aircraft and a round ricocheted into his leg. Despite being wounded, he turned the controls over to his copilot and was flown to Phu Bai, then evacuated through Cam Ranh Bay and Japan for further treatment.

Major Tharp returned to the United States on February 28, 1968, approximately three weeks after being wounded. The accompanying photograph shows his reunion with his wife, Mrs. John J. Tharp, and their children, John Jr., age 7, and Lori, at the Marine Corps Air Facility, New River, North Carolina.

The article recounts that before leaving for Vietnam, Tharp had reassured his family that he would return. His son John Jr. reportedly greeted him by saying, “No, Daddy, we just knew you would come home.”

title: Alma Tharp Bell – A Lifetime of Aviation and a Record-Setting Legacy
description:
Retrospective newspaper article by J. Douglas Donehue recounting the aviation career of Alma Edythe Tharp Bell. Alma made her first solo flight at age 16 and became one of the relatively few licensed women pilots active in South Carolina during the late 1940s and early 1950s. She frequently flew with fellow aviator and close friend Jewell Bailey in Alma's airplane, named “Rebel” after Charleston's South Atlantic League baseball team.

The article describes Alma and Jewell's involvement with The Ninety-Nines, the organization founded by Amelia Earhart and other women pilots. In 1949, Jewell Bailey set a light-airplane altitude record at the Azalea Festival, flying a Piper Cub to 26,875 feet, 1,112 feet above the previous record.

In 1947, Alma flew her father, Graham Tharp, to Atlanta to see a new Ercoupe. He liked the airplane so much that he purchased it for Alma. Alma later taught her father to fly and also taught her 14-year-old brother Johnny Tharp. In 1950, she served as an official hostess for the national Ninety-Nines convention in Greenville and was described as the organization's youngest member.

As Alma's reputation grew, she and Jewell Bailey became well known in regional aviation circles, flying to air shows throughout the Carolinas and Southeast. Alma grew up at Folly Beach, later married James Stewart “Buster” Bell Jr. in 1952, and moved to Lancaster. The article states that Alma was 67 years old when she died on May 19.

title: Alma Tharp Bell Memorial Obituary – 1994
description: Memorial obituary for Alma Tharp Bell, published in The Enterprise of High Point, North Carolina, on May 20, 1994. Alma died May 18, 1994, at age 67. Born in Charleston to Graham E. and Ethel Fike Tharp, she later lived in Lancaster, worked for Springs Industries, and was a member of Christ Episcopal Church. She was the widow of James Stewart Bell Jr. and was survived by her sons James S. Bell III and William R. “Dickey” Bell, along with her siblings and two grandchildren. Alma was buried at Lancaster Memorial Park.

title: Alma Tharp Bell Memorial – Twenty-Third Psalm – 1994
description: Memorial keepsake from the funeral of Alma Tharp Bell, who died May 18, 1994. The card features the Twenty-Third Psalm, surrounded by a floral border, with the words “Rest In Peace.” It was preserved with Alma’s obituary and funeral records as a remembrance of her life.

title: Alma Tharp Bell Obituary – May 1994
description: Newspaper obituary for Alma Tharp Bell, 67, of Lancaster, South Carolina, who died May 18, 1994. The notice identifies her as a Charleston County native, former Springs Industries employee, member of Christ Episcopal Church, and widow of James Stewart Bell Jr. It lists her sons James Bell III and William “Dickey” Bell, her brother Johnny Tharp, sisters Marion Brown and Rachel Bell, and two grandchildren. Funeral services were held at Mahaffey Funeral Home, with burial at Lancaster Memorial Park.

title: BQ1 – Gilliam-McConnell Airfield
description:
BQ1 is one of those airports that makes a great excuse to go flying. Located in Carthage, North Carolina, the real attraction is that you can land, park the airplane, and walk right over to the BBQ restaurant on the field.

It’s a perfect fly-in destination: grab some barbecue, watch airplanes come and go, and then head back home. Sometimes the best reason for a flight is simply BBQ at the end of the runway.

BQ1 – Fly in. Eat BBQ. Fly home.

title: The First Solo – Cutting the Shirt Tail
description:
One of aviation’s oldest traditions happens after a student pilot completes their first solo flight.

In the early days of flying, instructors often sat behind their students in tandem aircraft. With no radios or intercoms, the instructor would sometimes get the student’s attention by tugging on the back of their shirt. Once the student successfully flew alone, they no longer needed the instructor pulling on their shirttail.

So after that first solo, the instructor cuts the tail off the student pilot’s shirt.

The shirttail is usually dated and marked with the aircraft, airport, or other details from the flight and kept as a reminder of the accomplishment.

For a pilot, that cut shirt represents something much bigger than an old piece of fabric—it marks the first time you took an airplane up, flew it, and brought it safely back down completely on your own.

Your first solo is a flight you never forget.

title: Snorkeling for Scallops
description:
Scalloping is part treasure hunt, part fishing trip, and part underwater adventure. With a mask, snorkel, fins, and a mesh bag, you head into the clear, shallow water searching through the seagrass for bay scallops.

Once you spot one, you dive down and pick it up by hand—but watch your fingers, because they can snap their shells shut!

It’s a great way to spend a summer day on the water, and there’s nothing quite like bringing the day’s catch back to the boat and later enjoying fresh scallops that you collected yourself.

Swim. Search. Dive. Dinner.

title: Cedar Key, Florida – Fly-In Adventure
description:
Flying into Cedar Key, Florida is an adventure all by itself. The small island airport sits right along the Gulf, giving you beautiful views of the water and islands as you come in to land.

After tying down the airplane, you can head into town for fresh seafood, cold drinks, and that laid-back Old Florida atmosphere Cedar Key is known for.

It’s not about getting somewhere fast—it’s about enjoying the flight, the scenery, and arriving somewhere you probably wouldn't experience the same way by car.

Fly in. Eat seafood. Enjoy the island. Fly home.

title: KSSI – Fly-In BBQ
description:
KSSI – Fly-In BBQ

Sometimes the best flying destinations are the simple ones: an airplane, a runway, and good BBQ.

A flight into KSSI – St. Simons Island Airport combines the fun of flying with one of aviation’s favorite traditions—going somewhere just because there’s something good to eat when you get there.

Land the airplane, tie it down, grab some BBQ, enjoy St. Simons Island for a while, and then climb back in for the flight home.

Because pilots will fly a long way for good BBQ.
